summary: Describes version 2 of KeyNote, a trust-management system. It specifies the syntax and meaning of assertions, how action attributes are processed, and the application architecture a KeyNote implementation fits into. It lets policy and credentials decide whether an action is allowed. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking who you are, KeyNote asks whether a signed note says you may do this. It is like a permission slip that the guard checks.

questions: what is the policy principal in keynote
how does keynote compute compliance value
subtitle: A trust-management system where signed, programmable assertions decide whether an action is allowed.

tldr.problem: Applications need a standard way to specify security policy and credentials, rather than each inventing its own access control lists and certificate parsers.
tldr.mechanism: KeyNote uses one assertion language for both policies and credentials. An application sends a set of assertions, an action description made of name-value pairs and the requesting principals to a compliance checker, which returns a policy compliance value.
tldr.outcome: Applications get advice they can enforce, derived only positively from trusted assertions. The memo is Informational and leaves credential revocation to a future document.

today: RFC 2704 is an Informational memo from September 1999. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Trust Management and KeyNote
sections.content:
Trust management is a unified approach to specifying and interpreting security policies, credentials and relationships, allowing direct authorization of security-critical actions. Unlike traditional certificates that bind keys to names, trust-management credentials can bind keys directly to the authorization to perform specific tasks.

The RFC lists five components: a language for actions, a way to identify principals, a language for policies, a language for credentials, and a compliance checker that says how a requested action should be handled. KeyNote provides a single language for both local policies and credentials, called assertions. Applications talk to a locally trusted compliance checker through a function-call style interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Rather than checking a name tag, the guard reads a signed note that says exactly what you are allowed to do.

sections.title: Principals, Actions and Assertions
sections.content:
A principal may be a person, a process, a public key or any other convenient abstraction, identified by a string. Principals request actions and issue assertions. Actions are described to the checker as an action attribute set of name-value pairs built by the application. Names are case-sensitive and begin with a letter or underscore. KeyNote guarantees support for names and values up to 2048 characters.

The special principal POLICY is the root of trust and is authorized to do anything. Assertions issued by POLICY are policy assertions. When a principal is identified by a public key it can sign assertions, producing credentials that serve like certificates and can cross untrusted networks. By convention the app_domain attribute names the application domain, and attribute names beginning with an underscore are reserved for the runtime, such as _MIN_TRUST, _MAX_TRUST, _VALUES and _ACTION_AUTHORIZERS.

A key design principle is assertion monotonicity: removing an assertion never raises the compliance value, so a network failure that loses credentials can never cause spurious authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss at the top, called POLICY, hands out permission slips. Anyone holding a chain of slips back to the boss can do the thing. Losing a slip can only make you less allowed, never more.

sections.title: Assertion Syntax and Fields
sections.content:
An assertion is ASCII text in RFC 822-style fields, one field per line, with continuation lines indented. Authorizer is the only mandatory field. Optional fields are KeyNote-Version (which should be 2 for this document and appear first), Local-Constants, Licensees, Conditions, Comment and Signature (which appears last). Blank lines are not allowed inside an assertion.

  • Authorizer names the principal issuing the assertion.
  • Licensees names who is authorized, using &&, || and a K-of threshold construct.
  • Conditions is a small program of tests on the action attributes, with clauses of the form test -> value. It supports string, integer and floating point comparisons and POSIX regular expression matching with ~=.
  • Local-Constants defines short names, useful for long keys.
  • Signature is computed over the text up to the Signature field and requires a cryptographic Authorizer.

Cryptographic principal identifiers have the form ALGORITHM:ENCODEDBITS. Other identifiers are opaque labels.
sections.plainLanguage: An assertion is a short form with blanks to fill in: who is giving permission, who gets it, and under what conditions. A signature at the bottom proves who wrote it.

sections.title: Query Evaluation
sections.content:
A query has four parameters: the requesting principals, the action attribute set, the ordered set of compliance values (from _MIN_TRUST to _MAX_TRUST) and the assertions to use. The values can be Boolean such as {FALSE, TRUE} or a range such as {No_Access, Limited_Access, Full_Access}.

The policy compliance value is the compliance value of the principal POLICY. A principal's value is the maximum of its direct authorization value (_MAX_TRUST if it is a requesting authorizer, else _MIN_TRUST) and the values of all assertions it authorizes. An assertion's value is the minimum of its Conditions value (the maximum of its successful clauses) and its Licensees value. In a Licensees expression, && takes the minimum, || the maximum, and K-of takes the K-th highest value.

A clause with no value means _MAX_TRUST. A runtime error, such as division by zero or an invalid regular expression, makes that test false. How an implementation builds the delegation graph is implementation-dependent.
sections.plainLanguage: Follow the chain of slips from the boss down to the person asking. The answer can be no stronger than the weakest slip in the chain, and a person with several routes gets the best one.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two groups of examples. The first is an email certificate setup: a policy that fully trusts RSA key abc123, a credential in which that key trusts two keys as certification authorities for one email domain, and further credentials issued to specific users, each tested against the address and optional name attributes.

The second is a spending workflow. A policy lets the CFO's key approve amounts under 10000 in the SPEND domain. The CFO then delegates: any two signers including the vice president may approve under 7500 (logged from 2500 up), and a separate credential lets one signer approve under 500, logged when the amount is 100 or more. With compliance values {"Reject", "ApproveAndLog", "Approve"}, the RFC shows which requests come out as Approve, ApproveAndLog or Reject.

The RFC notes that the keys and signatures in its examples are fictitious and much shorter than real ones.
sections.plainLanguage: A company says the boss can spend a lot, the boss lets managers spend a little, and the checker works out whether a given purchase is okay, needs a note in the log, or is refused.

sections.title: Architecture, Limits and Security
sections.content:
KeyNote does not enforce policy; it only advises the application that calls it. The RFC says the action attributes must reflect the application's security needs, the policy must be correct, and the application itself must be trustworthy. Nothing stops an application from ignoring KeyNote or feeding it misleading assertions.

Choosing credentials is outside the language. Even inappropriate credentials cannot approve an illegal action, as long as the policy is correct and the attributes are passed correctly. KeyNote provides no revocation service, though credentials can include date tests to expire. A future document is to address expiration and revocation.

The formal Security Considerations section is brief: bugs in or incorrect use of a compliance checker could have security implications for every application that uses it. The IANA section covers three registries: app_domain names, public key format identifiers and signature algorithm identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: The checker only gives advice, like a friend saying whether the rules allow it. The program has to actually listen, and the rules have to be written correctly.

items.title: Authorizer
items.text: Mandatory. The principal issuing the assertion.

items.title: Licensees
items.text: The principals being authorized, with && , || and K-of.

items.title: Conditions
items.text: Tests on action attributes, each giving a compliance value.

items.title: Local-Constants
items.text: Short names for long values such as keys.

items.title: Signature
items.text: Makes the assertion a credential; always last.

viz.caption: EMAIL CERTIFICATE EXAMPLE FROM THE RFC

data.title: A KeyNote assertion
data.code:
KeyNote-Version: 2
Comment: A simple, if contrived, email certificate for user mab
Local-Constants:  ATT_CA_key = "RSA:acdfa1df1011bbac"
                  mab_key = "DSA:deadbeefcafe001a"
Authorizer: ATT_CA_key
Licensees: mab_key
Conditions: ((app_domain == "email")  # valid for email only
          && (address == "mab@research.att.com"));
Signature: "RSA-SHA1:f00f2244"
